title: The history of the microphone
tagline: About 170 years from a pig's bristle scratching soot to the four tiny silicon microphones inside your phone.
intro: A microphone does one job: it lets sound push on something light, and turns that push into electricity. The first ones were built for the telephone, and used loose grains of carbon that crackled and hissed. Radio, films and records then demanded something cleaner, so engineers tried a charged metal skin, a foil ribbon and a coil of wire in a magnet. Those same ideas are still at work today, on every stage, in every studio, and shrunk onto silicon chips made by the billion.

eras.name: Carbon and the telephone
eras.summary: Inventors learn that a thin skin can follow a voice, and that loose carbon can turn its movement into a changing electric current strong enough for a telephone line.

eras.name: Condensers and broadcasting
eras.summary: Radio, electrical recording and talking films need cleaner sound. The condenser microphone arrives, the ribbon is invented, and the best carbon microphones are carved into marble.

eras.name: Ribbons, coils and direction
eras.summary: Ribbon and moving-coil microphones go on sale, and engineers learn to make a microphone listen in one direction and ignore the rest. The great studio classics are born.

eras.name: Stage classics and the electret
eras.summary: A plastic film that holds its charge makes microphones tiny and cheap. Tough stage microphones, phantom power and the XLR cable become the standards still used today.

eras.name: Silicon and digital
eras.summary: Sound becomes numbers, and the microphone becomes a chip. Billions of microphones a year are now etched from silicon and built into phones, earbuds and speakers.

events.title: Sound draws its own picture
events.text: Scott patented the phonautograph. Sound went into a horn and shook a thin membrane, and a bristle fixed to the membrane scratched a wavy line on paper blackened with soot. In 1860 it traced someone singing ‘Au clair de la lune’. Nobody could play it back until 2008.
events.why: It proved that a thin skin can follow a sound wave exactly, which is the first step inside every microphone.

events.title: A teacher's ‘Telephon’
events.text: Reis showed the Physical Society of Frankfurt a device he called the Telephon. A parchment diaphragm pushed on a platinum contact, so the vibration changed an electric current. It carried musical notes well, but speech came through poorly.
events.why: It was an early attempt to make a diaphragm control electricity, and it gave the telephone its name.

events.title: ‘Mr. Watson, come here’
events.who: Alexander Graham Bell and Thomas Watson; Elisha Gray
events.text: Bell spoke into a liquid transmitter: a diaphragm moved a wire up and down in a small cup of liquid, which changed the current smoothly. Watson heard the words in the next room. Elisha Gray had described a liquid transmitter in a patent caveat filed on 14 February 1876, the same day as Bell's patent application, and people still argue about who thought of it first.
events.why: It showed that a current which rises and falls smoothly with the voice can carry speech, though a cup of liquid was no use in a real telephone.

events.title: Berliner and Edison race to a better transmitter
events.where: Washington, D.C., and Menlo Park, New Jersey, USA
events.text: Berliner, a young German immigrant, filed a patent for a loose-contact transmitter in June 1877, and the Bell company acquired it. Edison filed his own application for a carbon transmitter the same year. Edison's patent was not granted until 3 May 1892, and in 1901 a US appeals court ruled that Edison had come first.
events.why: The carbon transmitter gave a far stronger signal than Bell's own design, and it made the telephone practical.

events.title: The carbon microphone gets its name
events.text: Hughes found that a loose electrical contact, such as a nail resting on two others or a carbon pencil sitting between carbon blocks, changes its resistance with the faintest vibration. His paper was read to the Royal Society on 8 May 1878. He called the device a microphone, a word Charles Wheatstone had used in 1827 for a purely mechanical listening aid, and he chose not to patent it.
events.why: It explained why carbon works so well and gave the microphone its name.

events.title: A clergyman fills it with granules
events.who: Henry Hunnings, later Anthony C. White
events.text: Hunnings, a Yorkshire curate, patented a transmitter with loose carbon granules packed behind the diaphragm. It gave a clearer, stronger voice than other transmitters of its day. In 1892 the American engineer Anthony White patented the ‘solid-back’ version, which became the standard Bell transmitter and was used well into the 1930s.
events.why: Carbon granule microphones stayed inside telephones for about a hundred years.

events.title: The condenser microphone
events.text: Wente stretched a steel diaphragm about 22 thousandths of a millimetre thick a hair's width from a metal plate. Sound changed the gap, and that changed the electric charge the pair could hold. He filed his patent on 20 December 1916 and described the design in the Physical Review the next year. His model 394 capsule went into Western Electric's studio microphones.
events.why: It was the first truly high-quality microphone, and studios still use its descendants for vocals.

events.title: A microphone carved from marble
events.text: Working for Eugen Reisz in Berlin, the young Georg Neumann put carbon powder in a hollow in a block of marble and covered it with a thin membrane. Marconi built the design in Britain, and by 1927 it was in almost universal use at the BBC. It had to be turned each day so the carbon would not settle.
events.why: It was the best that carbon could do, and its limits pushed Neumann to start building condenser microphones.

events.title: A ribbon in a magnet
events.text: At Siemens, Schottky and Gerlach hung a very thin strip of aluminium in the gap of a magnet. Run a current through it and it moved and made sound. Let sound move it and it made a tiny current. They are credited with inventing the ribbon loudspeaker and the ribbon microphone, usually dated to 1924.
events.why: The ribbon is the lightest diaphragm of all, and it is also its own electrical conductor.

events.title: Radio reaches India
events.who: Indian Broadcasting Company, later All India Radio
events.text: After radio clubs began experiments in 1923, the Indian Broadcasting Company opened a station in Bombay on 23 July 1927 and one in Calcutta a month later. The government took the service over in 1930 and renamed it All India Radio on 8 June 1936. It grew from six stations at independence to hundreds.
events.why: For the first time a single voice at a microphone could be heard across a whole country.

events.title: The Neumann ‘bottle’
events.text: Neumann founded his own company in Berlin and built the CMV 3, a tall condenser microphone with a valve amplifier inside, nicknamed the bottle. It is described as the first mass-produced condenser microphone. From 1932 a newer version took screw-on capsule heads, including a one-directional one.
events.why: It took the condenser microphone out of the laboratory and into broadcast studios.

events.title: The moving-coil microphone goes on sale
events.where: Western Electric and Bell Labs, New York, USA
events.text: A loudspeaker run backwards is a microphone: sound pushes a dome, the dome moves a coil of wire in a magnet's field, and a voltage appears. Western Electric's 618A of 1931, by Wente and Thuras, is described as the first dynamic microphone made for commercial sale. British engineers had built a moving-coil studio microphone for the BBC as early as 1923.
events.why: The dynamic microphone needs no power supply and is very tough, which is why it rules the stage.

events.title: RCA's ribbon microphones
events.who: Harry F. Olson and Les Anderson
events.text: Olson turned the ribbon into a product. RCA made the PB-31 in 1931, and Radio City Music Hall was using it the next year. The Type 44-A followed (sources give 1931 to 1933), with a crimped metal ribbon only a few thousandths of a millimetre thick. It heard the front and the back equally and ignored the sides.
events.why: Its warm sound and figure-of-eight pattern shaped the voices of radio and film for decades.

events.title: Two microphones make stereo
events.text: Blumlein filed British patent 394,325 for what he called binaural sound. One of his ideas was to put two figure-of-eight microphones in the same spot, crossed at right angles. Each one hears mostly one side of the room.
events.why: The crossed pair is still called a Blumlein pair, and it shows how useful a directional microphone can be.

events.title: One capsule, two diaphragms
events.who: Hans Joachim von Braunmühl and Walter Weber
events.text: Two engineers at the German broadcasting company filed a patent for a condenser capsule with a diaphragm on each side of one back plate. It is described as the first one-directional condenser microphone. Change the voltage on the rear diaphragm and the pattern changes too.
events.why: This capsule became Neumann's M 7, and it is the reason a studio microphone can switch its pattern.

events.title: A microphone that points
events.text: Olson filed a patent in October 1938 for a ‘line microphone’: a bundle of pipes of different lengths in front of the capsule. Sound from the side arrives out of step through the pipes and cancels itself. Sennheiser says it showed a single-tube shotgun microphone in 1954, and its MD 82 of 1956 is often called the first practical one.
events.why: The shotgun microphone lets film and television crews pick up a voice from outside the picture.

events.title: The Unidyne hears one way
events.text: Bauer, a 25-year-old engineer born in Odessa, let sound reach the back of the diaphragm through small openings that delayed it a little. Sound from behind then pushed both sides at once and cancelled out. Shure calls its Unidyne Model 55 the first one-directional microphone with a single moving-coil element.
events.why: A heart-shaped pickup pattern ignores the loudspeakers behind it, which holds back the howl of feedback.

events.title: A sound company for India
events.text: Seven years before independence, A. N. Ahuja started work in Delhi as a sound contractor. His company began making its own public address equipment in 1942, opened a factory at Okhla in 1958 and exported to Burma from 1952. Ahuja microphones, amplifiers and horn speakers became a familiar sight at Indian weddings, rallies and school functions.
events.why: It shows the microphone becoming an everyday tool far from the laboratories where it was invented.

events.title: The Neumann U 47
events.text: Neumann showed a prototype at the Berlin Radio Show in 1947, and the earliest recorded sale was in December 1949. Its M 7 capsule had two diaphragms, and a switch chose between hearing one way and hearing all round. Frank Sinatra and the Beatles' producer George Martin were among those who relied on it.
events.why: It is often described as the first condenser microphone with a switchable pattern, and it set the sound of the modern vocal recording.

events.title: Lata Mangeshkar walks to the microphone
events.text: For the ghostly song ‘Aayega Aanewala’ in the film Mahal, the makers wanted a voice that seemed to drift in from far away. By Mangeshkar's own account, she started singing in a far corner of the studio and walked slowly towards the single microphone in the middle, reaching it as the main tune began. The song made her a star.
events.why: With one microphone and no effects, distance itself was the mixing desk.

events.title: Vienna's nine patterns
events.who: AKG: Rudolf Görike, Ernst Pless and Konrad Wolf
events.text: AKG was founded in Vienna in 1947. In 1953 it introduced the D12, a dynamic microphone that won it fans around the world, and the C12 condenser. The C12 came with a box that let the engineer choose any of nine pickup patterns from a distance, without touching the microphone.
events.why: Pattern became a control you could turn during a session, not a fixed property of the microphone.

events.title: Cutting the cable
events.who: Shure, and Sennheiser with the broadcaster NDR
events.text: Several inventors claim the first wireless microphone. Shure calls its Vagabond 88 of 1953 the first handheld wireless system for performers, though it was costly and had a short range. In 1957 Sennheiser and the broadcaster NDR showed a system that reached about 100 m, later sold as the Mikroport.
events.why: Performers could finally walk away from the microphone stand.

events.title: The XLR plug
events.text: Cannon's X series connector gained a latch by 1950, making it the XL. By 1955 the socket had springy rubber around its contacts, marked with an R. The three pins carry a shield and two copies of the signal, one of them upside down.
events.why: The balanced, locking XLR cable is still how almost every professional microphone is plugged in.

events.title: The electret: a charge that stays
events.text: A condenser microphone needed a high voltage to charge its diaphragm. Sessler and West used a thin Teflon film that holds an electric charge for good, like a magnet holds magnetism. Their patent, US 3,118,022, was granted on 14 January 1964.
events.why: Electret microphones were small, cheap and good, and the National Inventors Hall of Fame says they came to make up about 90% of all microphones made.

events.title: The SM57 and SM58
events.text: Seeler spent years on Shure's Unidyne III capsule of 1959, dropping and abusing prototypes until they survived. Shure put it in the SM57 in 1965 and, under a ball-shaped grille, in the SM58 in 1966. SM stood for studio microphone, but both ended up ruling the stage.
events.why: The SM58 is still called the most popular vocal microphone in the world, and the SM57 has stood on the US president's lectern since 1965.

events.title: Phantom power
events.who: Georg Neumann GmbH and Norwegian Broadcasting (NRK)
events.text: Neumann's new transistor microphone, the KM 84, took its power down the same cable that carried its sound. The Norwegian broadcaster already had 48 volts in its studios for emergency lighting, so 48 volts it was. The voltage sits equally on both signal wires, so a microphone that does not need it never notices.
events.why: 48 volt phantom power became a world standard, and it is on almost every mixer and audio interface today.

events.title: Sound becomes numbers
events.text: The ‘Red Book’ standard for the compact disc was published in 1980. It measures the microphone's signal 44,100 times a second and stores each measurement as a 16-bit number. The first discs reached shops in Japan on 1 October 1982.
events.why: From here on, what a microphone hears is usually turned into numbers within a few centimetres of cable.

events.title: A microphone made of silicon
events.text: Sessler, by then a professor in Germany, and his student Hohm applied for a patent on a condenser microphone built on a silicon chip. Their first prototype was a square 10 mm on each side. By 1989 a Darmstadt design measured about 2 mm.
events.why: It showed that a microphone could be made with the same tools as a computer chip.

events.title: MEMS microphones reach the factory
events.text: Knowles, a maker of hearing aid parts, launched the SiSonic: a silicon microphone that a robot could solder onto a circuit board like any other chip. An electret capsule could not take that heat. Knowles shipped its billionth in August 2009 and its ten billionth by early 2017.
events.why: Microphones became as cheap and as easy to fit as any other chip, so designers started using several at once.

events.title: A second microphone to cancel noise
events.text: The iPhone 4 had two microphones: one by your mouth and one at the top. The top one listened to the room so that a chip could subtract the background noise from your voice. Recent iPhones are reported to carry four microphones.
events.why: With several microphones and some arithmetic, a phone can choose what to listen to, which is a polar pattern made in software.

people.name: Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville
people.note: Made the first recordings of sound, as wavy lines traced by a diaphragm and a bristle.

people.name: David Edward Hughes
people.note: Showed how loose carbon contacts pick up sound, named the microphone and refused to patent it.

people.name: Emile Berliner
people.note: Sold an early telephone transmitter to Bell, and later invented the flat gramophone disc.

people.name: Edward C. Wente
people.note: Invented the condenser microphone and co-designed the first dynamic microphone sold commercially.

people.name: Walter Schottky
people.note: Co-invented the ribbon microphone at Siemens with Erwin Gerlach.

people.name: Georg Neumann
people.note: Went from a marble carbon microphone to the CMV 3 and the U 47.

people.name: Harry F. Olson
people.note: Designed RCA's ribbon microphones and patented the line microphone, ancestor of the shotgun.

people.name: Alan Blumlein
people.note: Invented stereo recording with a crossed pair of microphones; died testing radar in the war.

people.name: Walter Weber
people.note: With Hans Joachim von Braunmühl, designed the two-diaphragm capsule behind switchable patterns.

people.name: Benjamin Bauer
people.note: Arrived in America at 17 speaking little English, and at 25 invented the Unidyne's one-way pickup.

people.name: A. N. Ahuja
people.note: Started as a sound contractor in Delhi and built India's best known public address brand.

people.name: Lata Mangeshkar
people.note: Recorded thousands of film songs, and used her distance from the microphone as part of the performance.

people.name: James E. West
people.note: Co-invented the electret microphone at Bell Labs and has pushed for more diversity in science.

people.name: Gerhard Sessler
people.note: Co-invented both the electret microphone and, twenty years later, the silicon microphone.

series.title: Silicon microphones shipped by one company
series.caption: Knowles' own announcements of how many SiSonic MEMS microphones it had shipped in total: the first billion took six years, and the ninth and tenth took about one.

facts: David Hughes never patented his microphone. He thought everyone should be free to build on it.
The BBC's marble microphones of the late 1920s had to be turned every day, to stop the carbon inside from settling.
Phantom power is 48 volts because Norwegian radio studios already had a 48 volt supply for their emergency lights.
Ernie Seeler, who designed the capsule in the SM57 and SM58, expected it to record orchestras and is said to have disliked rock music.
The oldest known recording of a voice, traced in soot in 1860, was not heard until a laboratory scanned it in 2008.
Every US president since Lyndon Johnson has given speeches through a Shure SM57.
